entry.title: GLM-5.3 on Workers AI sent 155 replies with other customers' text, all with HTTP 200
entry.summary: Cloudflare's 26 October report: prompts over 681,280 tokens got answers built partly from other users' requests, with a normal status and token count. A canary test catches what a status code cannot; ours costs cents.
entry.content:
From 27 August to 9 September 2026, Cloudflare's hosted copy of the GLM-5.3 model answered 155 requests with text that belonged to other customers' requests 1. Every one of those prompts was longer than 681,280 tokens. The replies came back with HTTP 200, a token count that matched the long prompt, and coherent text 1. Nothing in the response said anything was wrong. Cloudflare and the maintainers of SGLang, the open-source engine that runs the model, published the details together on 26 October 12.

Two settings that disagreed, and an engine that did not object

A language model keeps a working memory of the prompt it is reading, called the KV cache. On a shared server that memory is a pool of fixed-size pages, handed to one request and then reused by the next. Pages are not wiped between requests; the next request writes over them 1.

Cloudflare runs GLM-5.3 in disaggregated mode: one set of GPUs reads the prompt and fills the cache (prefill), then sends the pages to a second set that writes the answer (decode) 1. The model page advertised a 1,048,576-token context window 5, but the prefill pool had room for 681,280 tokens. Cloudflare knew about the gap before launch and expected the engine to refuse anything that did not fit 1.

The engine did refuse it, on paper. It marked the long request as rejected and swapped the prompt for a one-token placeholder. The admission queues checked whether a request had finished, not whether it had been rejected, so the request went ahead. Prefill wrote one page and reported the transfer complete. Decode had reserved pages for the full prompt and read all of them: one fresh page, the rest still holding earlier users' prompts and answers 1.

On a single server the same rejection returned an error; the leak needed the split between prefill and decode 2.

The bug was public before the model launched

Date (2026)Event
6 JulyIssue #30233 opened on SGLang: over-long prompts in disaggregated mode produce garbage from an incomplete cache 3
27 AugustGLM-5.3 launches on Workers AI with the smaller prefill pool 1
5 SeptemberIssue #30233 closed by a bot for inactivity 3
8 September, 23:11 UTCResearcher Gadi Evron of Knostic reports the leak through HackerOne 1
9 September, 14:00 UTCModel set to private; requests return HTTP 400 1
9 September, 19:40 UTCModel restored with a larger pool and a patched engine 1
19 OctoberSGLang v0.5.22 released 4
26 OctoberCoordinated publication 12

Cloudflare's fix was to make the pool hold about 2.04 million tokens, twice the context window, so a valid prompt cannot reach the rejection path, and to patch the engine so a rejected request stops before any transfer 1. Cloudflare reports no other Workers AI model affected and no sign of deliberate exploitation 1.

The same family of bug is wider than one model

The SGLang post describes a second, related flaw: a request cancelled while its cache pages are still in flight between machines can leave writes landing in pages already given to someone else 2. It affected default disaggregated setups from the v0.4 line, early 2025, until v0.5.21 (v0.5.22 for the MORI transfer backend), and the fixes were not backported to older release branches 2. The corruption is silent, so an operator cannot tell afterwards whether it happened 2.

If you run SGLang yourself with prefill and decode on separate machines:

  1. Read the KV pool size from each node's startup log and compare it with the context length you advertise, after every change to weights, quantization or parallelism. If the pool is smaller, lower the context length 1.
  2. Upgrade to v0.5.22 or later 14.
  3. Turn on --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum on both prefill and decode where your model supports it. It is off by default because it adds work to every transfer 2. Cloudflare says it does not yet cover GLM-5.3, GLM-5.3 Flash or DeepSeek V4 1.

A single-server deployment without cross-machine transfer is outside this particular race 2.

A status code cannot catch this; a canary can

Cloudflare's own pre-launch tests passed because they checked status codes and speed at long contexts, not whether the answer matched the prompt 1. A canary test checks the answer: hide strings in a long prompt that only you know, ask for them back, and compare. In the GLM-5.3 bug only the first cache page held the request's own prompt, so strings placed further in would have gone missing from the reply.

We ran one on 2 November 2026 through Workers AI. Three random codes sat at 10%, 50% and 90% of a filler text, with a made-up final word, and the model was asked to return all four. Three prompt sizes, three models, 26 calls.

ModelPrompt tokens billedRunsCodes returnedFinal word returned
GLM-5.31,632 to 1,64539 of 93 of 3
GLM-5.315,526 to 15,60739 of 93 of 3
GLM-5.377,463 to 77,56126 of 62 of 2
GLM-5.3 Flash1,632 to 77,508824 of 247 of 8
DeepSeek V4 Flash 07311,580 to 75,081927 of 278 of 9

All 78 codes came back. The two misses were at about 77,000 tokens: each model returned only the tail "zz" of the final word, a reading slip, not someone else's text. The 26 calls cost US$0.46. They stop at 77,000 tokens, far below the 681,280 where GLM-5.3 broke, so they show the method, not that long prompts are safe today; one canary at 700,000 tokens on GLM-5.3 would cost about US$0.98 at its list price of US$1.40 per million input tokens, read 2 November 2026 6.

import json, os, random, urllib.request

ACCOUNT, TOKEN = os.environ["CF_ACCOUNT_ID"], os.environ["CF_API_TOKEN"]
URL = f"https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/{ACCOUNT}/ai/v1/chat/completions"

def canary(model, n_words):
    words = [random.choice("river lamp stone rice bridge paper".split()) for _ in range(n_words)]
    codes = [f"{random.randint(0, 99999):05d}-{random.choice('ABCDEFGH')}" for _ in range(3)]
    for pos, code in zip((0.1, 0.5, 0.9), codes):
        words.insert(int(len(words) * pos), f". The code is {code}. ")
    prompt = "Reply with one line: the three codes in order.\n\n" + " ".join(words)
    body = json.dumps({"model": model, "max_tokens": 4096,
                       "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}).encode()
    req = urllib.request.Request(URL, body, {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}",
                                             "Content-Type": "application/json"})
    reply = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=600))
    text = reply["choices"][0]["message"]["content"] or ""
    return all(c in text for c in codes), reply["usage"]["prompt_tokens"]

print(canary("@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3", 15000))

Run it at the prompt sizes your app sends, on each model you use, after the host announces a new model or a new context window. A wrong answer with a 200 status is the signal to stop sending long prompts to that model and write to the host. Hongdam tests chatbots for weak points like this and writes the fixes 7.

entry.title: The week: Supabase stops exposing new tables, Brotli exploited, Mistral Large 4 weights
entry.summary: Six notes this week: a faster DeepSeek, a cap for Lovable's agent tools, Magento PolyShell, GitHub's US$50 default, Thai tokens, link cards. Plus four outside changes that reach a builder's app this month.
entry.content:
Since 30 October, a new table in a Supabase project is invisible to the app's API until someone grants access to it. Supabase announced the change in April and set Friday, 30 October, as the day it reaches every existing project 1. For an app built with Lovable, Bolt or another AI tool, the first sign is a 42501 error on a table the tool created this weekend. That change leads the four outside links below. First, the week's six notes.

Six notes, 26 to 31 October

Monday, models. DeepSeek Flash 1017 on Workers AI: DeepSeek's 17 October update promised shorter answers. On 10 builder tasks, 3 runs each, it finished in 40% less time than V4 Flash 0731 but wrote 23% more tokens. The lower price per token kept the bill level, and both models answered all 120 runs correctly. An output cap set for 0731 needs headroom on 1017.

Tuesday, last-mile. A per-user cap for Lovable's agent tools: Lovable's docs say its agent tools (the actions an AI assistant can call in your app) have no call quota and no call log. One Postgres table and one function cap calls per user, log each one, and turn a retried write into a no-op. Tested: 20 of 25 calls through, retries and calls with no signed-in user stopped.

Wednesday, security. Magento PolyShell on CISA's exploited list: CVE-2026-48356 lets a stranger upload a PHP file to a Magento shop through the guest cart. Attacks began in March, the fix for 2.4.8 and older came in July, and CISA listed it on 27 October. Patching does not remove a skimmer already in the shop's content blocks; the note gives four checks for that.

Thursday, automation. GitHub Agentic Workflows' default cap: the agent job gets a read-only token, and a separate job carries out the writes the workflow allows. A workflow with no cap of its own may spend US$10 a run and US$50 a day on AI, about US$1,500 a month. Three lines in the settings block lower it.

Friday, models. Thai tokens cost by model: the same eight shop messages took 1.46 times the English token count in Thai on DeepSeek, 2.64 times on Kimi K2.7 Code and 2.94 times on GLM-5.3. That reorders the price list: GLM-5.3 Flash lists at half DeepSeek's input price and comes out level for Thai text.

Saturday, last-mile. Link cards on Mastodon and Bluesky: every Mastodon server that receives a post fetches the page itself, reads only raw HTML (no JavaScript runs), and shows a wide picture only when it is wider than tall. Bluesky copies the card into the post once and never refreshes it. Three curl commands show what each one sees.

Supabase: a new table needs a grant before the API can see it

A grant is a Postgres permission that lets a role, such as anon (a visitor with no session) or authenticated (a signed-in user), touch a table at all. Row-level security, the rule that decides which rows a role sees, is a separate layer and works as before 1. Until Friday a Supabase project granted select, insert, update and delete on every new public table to those roles automatically 1.

From 30 October, on every project, a new table needs explicit grant lines; tables that existed before keep their grants 1. A missing grant returns error 42501, "permission denied", with a hint that spells out the GRANT to run 1. An app that talks to Postgres over a direct connection string is not affected 1.

The fix is three steps in the same migration: grant only what each role needs, turn on row-level security, then add the policies 1. Pasting the hint's GRANT without the other two opens its rows to anyone with the public key, the failure our 24 October note measured. Supabase's own reason for the change: AI tools and scripts now create tables with no person reading the diff 1.

Brotli 1.2.1 fixes a flaw attackers already use

Brotli is Google's compression library, the format behind Content-Encoding: br on the web 3. CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its exploited list on 27 October: a crafted compressed stream can corrupt the decoder's memory, leak it, crash it, or possibly run code, with no login 2. The fix is release v1.2.1, published 21 October 3; the Python package Brotli 1.2.1 reached PyPI on 22 October 4. US federal agencies must act by 10 November 2.

To find it, search the lockfile (requirements.txt, poetry.lock, package-lock.json) for brotli and check the system package with your distribution's package manager. Anything that decompresses Brotli sent by strangers, such as an upload handler or a proxy, comes first.

PHP2Shell now chains to root

The two PHP flaws from our 24 October note, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, joined CISA's list on 26 October with a three-day deadline 2. On 28 October CISA added a Linux kernel flaw, CVE-2026-46300, and its entry says attackers chain it with the two PHP flaws to plant PHP webshells (a small program left behind to run commands later) and run commands as root 2. The kernel deadline was 31 October 2. A PHP host patched for PHP2Shell and not yet for the kernel holds half the fix; the CISA entry lists the kernel commits 2.

Mistral Large 4 weights: free to run, a licence to resell

Mistral's 1-trillion-parameter model, about 50 billion active per token, with a 1-million-token context, now has its weights on Hugging Face; the files were last changed on 29 October 57. The licence is a modified MIT licence with one condition: a company that runs a "Model as a Service" business, meaning it gives others API or hosted access with meaningful control over inputs or training, needs a separate commercial licence from Mistral before commercial use 6. Internal use, and products that embed the model inside a specific feature, do not 6. A quantised NVFP4 copy targets NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs 5. A chatbot inside your own product reads as the embedded case; selling API access to the model is the case that needs Mistral's licence 6.

entry.title: Link cards: each Mastodon server fetches your page, Bluesky freezes the card
entry.summary: Mastodon 4.7.4 reads only the first 1 MB of raw HTML, only og:image, and shows a wide picture only when it is wider than tall. Bluesky copies the card into the post once. What each needs, with three curl checks.
entry.content:
A link card is the box with a picture, a title and a line of text that appears under a post when it contains a link. Mastodon and Bluesky build it in opposite ways. On Mastodon, every server that receives the post fetches your page itself. On Bluesky, the poster's app fetches it once and stores the card inside the post. A page that works on one can come out blank on the other, and the fixes differ.

Everything below comes from reading the code of Mastodon 4.7.4 (released 29 October 2026) and of the Bluesky app, not from their help pages. The measurements at the end come from five of our own notes, measured 31 October 2026.

Mastodon reads raw HTML: no JavaScript runs

Mastodon asks for the page with Accept: text/html and a user agent (the name a program sends with each request) that ends in Bot 1. It keeps the response only when the server answers 200 and the type is text/html, then parses the HTML as text 12. No browser renders it, so tags that a single-page app (a site whose pages are drawn by JavaScript in the browser) adds after loading are invisible. A route that a static host serves through its 404 page, a common trick for such apps, answers 404 and gets no card at all.

It reads at most 1 megabyte of the response 3. Tags placed after a large inline script or stylesheet can fall past that line.

Mastodon's tag rules

Card partWhere Mastodon reads it 2
TitleJSON-LD headline first, then og:title, then <title>
TextJSON-LD description first, then og:description, then <meta name="description">
Pictureog:image only; twitter:image is not read
Picture textog:image:alt
Address<link rel="canonical"> or og:url, used only on the same domain as the page
Author bylinefediverse:creator, an account such as @name@server

JSON-LD is structured data in a <script type="application/ld+json"> block, mostly written for search engines. Mastodon uses it only when the top-level object is a NewsArticle or a WebPage 2. The @graph form that many SEO plugins write is skipped, and the Open Graph tags win. A top-level WebPage block with its own headline replaces your og:title on the card.

The picture must be JPEG, PNG, GIF or WebP and under 8 MB 4. An SVG or a larger file leaves the card without a picture: Mastodon saves the card anyway and drops the image 4. Mastodon shrinks what it keeps to about 230,400 pixels, 640 × 360 4.

A wide picture needs to be wider than tall

The web interface shows the large, full-width card only when the stored picture's width is greater than its height, and crops it to 1.91 : 1 5. A square logo gets the small square thumbnail beside the text. A 1200 × 630 image, the usual Open Graph size, is 1.90 : 1 and fills the frame.

Every server fetches, and caches for two weeks

When a post arrives from another server, Mastodon queues the card fetch at a random moment within the next minute 6. Each server that receives the post does this on its own, so a post that reaches many servers brings one fetch from each, spread over about a minute, all with the Bot user agent. A firewall rule or bot filter that blocks them leaves those servers with no card.

Each server keeps a card per address and fetches it again only when it is more than two weeks old or lost its picture 1. Mastodon does not build a card for a post that already has a photo or a quote attached 1.

Bluesky freezes the card into the post

The Bluesky app asks a Bluesky service, cardyb.bsky.app, to read the page while the poster is writing 7. The app uploads the picture into the post itself; the post format accepts at most 1,000,000 bytes for it 8. After that the card is part of the post. A fixed og:image or a new title shows on new posts only; old posts keep what the page said when they were written.

Measured: our five latest notes

Note pageHTMLPosition of first og:image tagPicturecardyb, median of 3
DeepSeek Flash 101731.1 KBbyte 1,8721200 × 630 JPEG, 94 KB1.27 s
Lovable agent tools31.9 KBbyte 1,8541200 × 630 JPEG, 89 KB1.23 s
Magento PolyShell33.3 KBbyte 1,8381200 × 630 JPEG, 93 KB1.23 s
GitHub Agentic Workflows31.1 KBbyte 1,8421200 × 630 JPEG, 92 KB1.25 s
Thai tokens29.9 KBbyte 1,8301200 × 630 JPEG, 92 KB1.20 s

Each page answered 200 as text/html to a Mastodon-style request, and cardyb returned a title and a picture for each. Our pages carry their JSON-LD in an @graph, so Mastodon reads their Open Graph tags.

Three checks before you post a link

Replace the address and run these in a terminal. The first prints the status code, the type and the size Mastodon gets. The second lists the tags inside Mastodon's first megabyte. The third shows what Bluesky's card service sees.

URL=https://example.com/your-page/
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{content_type} %{size_download}\n' -A 'Mastodon/4.7.4 Bot' -H 'Accept: text/html' "$URL"
curl -s -A 'Mastodon/4.7.4 Bot' "$URL" | head -c 1048576 | grep -o '<meta[^>]*"\(og:[a-z:]*\|fediverse:creator\)"[^>]*>'
curl -s "https://cardyb.bsky.app/v1/extract?url=$(python3 -c 'import urllib.parse,sys;print(urllib.parse.quote(sys.argv[1],safe=""))' "$URL")"

A first line other than 200 text/html, an empty second command, or an empty image in the third each explains a blank card. For an app built in Lovable, Bolt or Replit, the usual fix is to write the Open Graph tags into the HTML the server sends, per page, rather than adding them with JavaScript after the page loads.

entry.title: Same text, Thai or English: 1.46 times the tokens on DeepSeek, 2.94 times on GLM-5.3
entry.summary: We sent the same eight shop messages in English, Thai and Chinese to six open models on Workers AI. Thai took 1.46 times the English tokens on DeepSeek and 2.94 times on GLM, enough to change which model is cheapest.
entry.content:
A price list for language models quotes dollars per million tokens. A token is the piece of text a model reads or writes: a whole word, part of a word, or a single letter. The same Thai sentence breaks into a different number of tokens on each model, so the price list does not tell a Thai shop what a model costs. On 30 October 2026 we sent eight short shop messages, each in English, Thai and Chinese, to six open models on Cloudflare Workers AI and read the token count each model billed. Thai came out at 1.46 times the English count on the three DeepSeek models, 2.64 times on Kimi K2.7 Code, and 2.94 times on the two GLM-5.3 models.

The tokenizer, not the model, sets the multiple

A tokenizer is the part of a model that cuts text into tokens before the model sees it. Many are built by byte-pair encoding: start from single characters, then keep merging the pair that appears most often in the training text until the vocabulary is full 2. A language that was common in that text gets long merged pieces; a language that was rare stays in short pieces. Petrov and colleagues measured this across many languages in 2023 and found the same text taking up to 15 times as many tokens from one language to another 3.

Our numbers fit that picture. The three DeepSeek models (V4 Flash 0731, V4.1 Flash 1017, V4 Pro 0813) billed the same count for every one of the 24 texts, and so did the two GLM-5.3 models. Within a family the multiple does not change with model size.

ModelEnglishThaiChineseThai ÷ EnglishChinese ÷ English
DeepSeek V4 Flash 07314286233741.460.87
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 10174286233741.460.87
DeepSeek V4 Pro 08134286233741.460.87
Kimi K2.7 Code4281,1323452.640.81
GLM-5.34331,2723822.940.88
GLM-5.3 Flash4331,2723822.940.88

Tokens for all eight texts together, prompt instruction subtracted. Measured 30 October 2026.

Per text, Thai ran from 1.27 to 1.59 times English on DeepSeek, 2.40 to 3.00 on Kimi and 2.55 to 3.47 on GLM. Chinese took fewer tokens than English on every model. Thai is shorter than English on the page (1,410 characters against 1,815 for the same eight texts), so the extra tokens come from how the tokenizer cuts Thai, not from length.

The Thai price reorders the price list

Multiply each model's input price 1 by its Thai multiple and you get what a million tokens' worth of English content costs once it is written in Thai.

Three changes from the English price list:

  • GLM-5.3 Flash lists at US$0.15 per million input tokens, half of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 at US$0.30 1. For Thai the two come out level at US$0.44.
  • Kimi K2.7 Code lists below DeepSeek V4 Pro (US$0.95 against US$1.32 1). For Thai, Kimi costs more: US$2.51 against US$1.92.
  • GLM-5.3 lists at US$1.40, close to DeepSeek V4 Pro 1. For Thai it costs more than twice as much.

The reply is cut by the same tokenizer, so a Thai answer should carry a similar multiple on the output price, which is 3 to 4.2 times the input price on these six models 1. We did not measure Thai replies today. Context windows shrink the same way: a GLM model holds about a third as much Thai as English.

Count your own text before you pick a model

Workers AI takes requests in the OpenAI format 4, and every reply we read today carried usage.prompt_tokens, the input count. Send one of your own messages with a one-word instruction, then send the instruction alone, and subtract:

curl -s "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$CF_ACCOUNT_ID/ai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CF_API_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash", "max_tokens": 1024,
       "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the single word OK.\n\nสวัสดีค่ะ อยากสั่งเมล็ดกาแฟคั่ว 2 ถุง"}]}' \
  | jq .usage.prompt_tokens

Leave max_tokens at 1,024 or more. Kimi and GLM-5.3 think before they answer, and with a 64-token allowance many of our first calls to them came back empty because the thinking used it all. An empty reply returned no count; we ran those again at 1,024.

Use a sample of the text your app handles: chat from your LINE account, product pages, support emails. The multiple moves with the kind of text: from 2.55 to 3.47 on GLM across our eight. Hongdam sets up chat assistants that answer customers from your own web pages 5.

How we measured

Eight passages a Chiang Rai business writes: a coffee order, a returns policy, a password-reset reply, a scarf description, a room offer, meeting notes, a menu item and a job post, 352 English words in all. We wrote each in Thai and Chinese ourselves. Each went to the six models with the instruction "Reply with the single word OK." in front, and we subtracted the count for the instruction alone (11 tokens on DeepSeek, 15 on Kimi, 19 on GLM). That is 150 calls, on 30 October 2026, through Workers AI's chat endpoint. A repeated GLM-5.3 call returned the same count. We measured cost, not quality; which model answers Thai customers best is a separate test.

entry.title: GitHub Agentic Workflows: the default spending cap is US$50 a day per workflow
entry.summary: GitHub Agentic Workflows reached general availability on 28 October 2026. The agent job gets no write access to your repository, but a workflow with no cap of its own may spend up to US$10 a run and US$50 a day on AI.
entry.content:
GitHub Agentic Workflows became generally available on 28 October 2026, for GitHub Free, Team and Enterprise 1. Version 1.0.1 of its command-line tool, gh aw, came out on 27 October 2. It lets a coding agent (an AI model that reads files and runs commands) do repository chores inside GitHub Actions: sort new issues, explain a failed build, update the docs, open a pull request.

The safety design holds up when you read the files it generates. The spending defaults are loose: a workflow that sets no cap of its own can spend up to 1,000 AI Credits a run and 5,000 a day, and one AI Credit is US$0.01 6. That is US$10 a run, US$50 a day, about US$1,500 a month per workflow. None of the five sample workflows GitHub keeps in its own example repository sets a lower cap 5.

You write a page of English, GitHub runs about 2,000 lines of YAML

You write a Markdown file: a short settings block, then instructions in plain English. gh aw compile turns it into a .lock.yml file, an ordinary GitHub Actions workflow, and both files go into the repository 3.

We read the five compiled workflows in the .github/workflows folder of githubnext/agentics, the project's example repository, on 29 October 2026 (commit 139fa09, compiled by gh-aw v0.93.3) 5. We parsed each file and counted its jobs, its steps and the write permissions of each job.

WorkflowSource linesCompiled linesJobsSteps
daily-repo-goals1992,2556131
daily-workflow-sync1501,8765110
import-workflow1981,8195109
link-checker2362,1856130
maintainer1021,9066114

The compiled file is the one that runs. Its header says not to edit it; you edit the Markdown and compile again. A pull request that changes a workflow therefore carries a diff of hundreds of generated lines, and the reviewer reads the Markdown change instead.

The agent job gets a read-only token

In all five files the job that runs the agent holds a single write permission, copilot-requests, which pays for the AI calls. Its token can read code, issues and pull requests; it cannot push code, open an issue or comment. Writes to the repository (contents, issues, pull-requests) sit in two other jobs, safe_outputs and conclusion 5.

One exception. The agent job also reads two optional repository secrets, GH_AW_GITHUB_TOKEN and GH_AW_GITHUB_MCP_SERVER_TOKEN 5. A personal access token (a password-like key tied to your own account) stored under either name keeps whatever scopes you gave it. Give it read scopes only.

This is the design GitHub calls safe outputs: the agent writes requests, and a separate job with the narrow permission carries out the ones the workflow allows, each type with a count limit 4. With no safe-outputs block, the only write allowed is one new issue 4. Between the two sits a detection job, which scans every proposed change before it is applied 1.

Every third-party step in the five files is pinned to a full 40-character commit, not a tag, and every container image to a digest (a fingerprint of its exact contents) 5. A tag can be moved to point at different code; a commit cannot.

The money sits in the AI Credits, not the runner minutes

A run pays twice: GitHub Actions minutes for the machine, and the AI provider for the model 6.

  • Minutes. A standard Linux runner costs US$0.006 a minute, and GitHub rounds each job up to a whole minute 7. The project's own estimate for an issue-triage workflow with 20 runs a month is about 10 minutes, about US$0.06 6. Standard runners in public repositories are free; GitHub Free includes US$12 of minutes a month for private ones 8.
  • AI Credits. Defaults: 1,000 per run and 5,000 per workflow per 24 hours 6. The detection job has its own cap of 400 per run 6. Whether detection counts toward the daily 5,000 is not stated on the page.

The AI Credit count is the tool's own estimate. The project says it may not match what the provider bills 6. The provider's invoice is the final number.

Three lines in the settings block set your own ceiling

Each of these is a top-level field in the Markdown file's settings block 6:

max-ai-credits: 200        # US$2 a run
max-daily-ai-credits: 500  # US$5 a day for this workflow
max-turns: 20              # at most 20 agent turns

Then run gh aw compile again and commit both files. Two more settings cut the number of runs that reach the model at all 6:

  • skip-if-match and skip-if-no-match under on: run a GitHub search in the first, cheap job; when it matches (or does not), the agent job never starts and no AI Credits are spent. Example: skip issues already labelled duplicate.
  • A schedule or a manual trigger (workflow_dispatch) is easier to budget than push, which fires on every push 6.

gh aw forecast, no longer experimental since the general-availability release, prints a monthly range of AI Credit spend for a workflow, detection included 1. Run it before you merge a new workflow.

For a founder

A triage bot that runs on every new issue and stays under its cap costs cents a month in minutes. The same bot on a busy public repository, on the defaults, can reach US$50 a day before it stops. Set max-daily-ai-credits to what you would pay a person for the same job.

entry.title: Magento PolyShell joins CISA's exploited list, seven months after the first attacks
entry.summary: CVE-2026-48356 lets anyone upload a PHP file to a Magento store through the guest cart. Attacks began in March; the fix for 2.4.8 and older came in July; CISA listed it on 27 October. Four checks find a break-in.
entry.content:
On 27 October 2026 CISA (the US government's cybersecurity agency) added CVE-2026-48356 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, the list of flaws it has evidence attackers use 1. The flaw, which the security firm Sansec named PolyShell, lets a stranger who has not logged in upload a file of their choosing to a Magento or Adobe Commerce shop 6. Sansec recorded the first attacks on 19 March 2026 6. Read this morning, 28 October, Adobe's bulletin still says Adobe is "not aware of any exploits in the wild" 3.

Magento Open Source is the free shop software; Adobe Commerce is the paid edition of the same code. A CVE number is the public ID of one flaw. A webshell is a small program an attacker leaves on a server to run commands on it later.

The guest cart accepts a PHP file dressed as a picture

Magento lets a product carry a "file" option, such as a logo for a printed mug. Its REST API (the address apps use to talk to the shop) takes that file inside a cart request, as base64 text with a name and a type, and writes it to pub/media/custom_options/quote/ 6. Two routes for guest carts, POST /V1/guest-carts/:cartId/items and PUT /V1/guest-carts/:cartId/items/:itemId, need no login. GraphQL, the shop's other API, takes a different path and is not affected 6.

Sansec lists three missing checks: the option ID is not matched to the product, the upload runs whether or not the product has a file option, and .php, .phtml and .phar names pass. The only test is whether the bytes start like an image, and a polyglot (a file that is a valid GIF and valid PHP at once) passes it 6. Whether the uploaded PHP then runs depends on the web server: stock nginx setups for Magento 2.0 to 2.2, nginx configured to hand every .php request to PHP, and Apache before 2.3.5 without php_flag engine 0 6.

Seven months from first attack to the exploited list

Date (2026)EventSource
17 MarchSansec publishes its warning6
19 MarchFirst attacks seen6
30 March471 stores compromised in one hour7
14 AprilSansec: 82% of all stores hit with malicious uploads6
12 MayMagento 2.4.9 released; Sansec states it carries the fix6
14 JulyAPSB26-73 brings fixes to 2.4.4 to 2.4.936
24 OctoberSansec ties the flaw to a skimmer campaign8
27 OctoberCISA adds CVE-2026-48356; US federal agencies must act by 10 November12

Between 12 May and 14 July, a shop on 2.4.8 or older had no fix from Adobe short of a move to 2.4.9 6. Sansec does not say which set of stores its 82% is a share of 6.

Adobe's bulletin rates the flaw Critical, priority 2, with a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.6 out of 10 3; NVD, the US vulnerability database, lists 9.3 with the same attack path but no harm to uptime 5. Both mark it as needing no login 35. The CISA feed marks ransomware use as unknown 2.

A patched store can still carry the attacker

Patching closes the door; it does not remove what came through it. Sansec found an attacker's script in the content blocks of 83 stores in October, loaded from deepveindrilling.com, and counts 953 stores hit by the same operator since July 2025 8. The script lives in the database table cms_block, the static blocks Magento prints into shop pages, and keeps a copy of itself in the shopper's browser storage, so it runs again even when its home domain goes down 8. On 23 October it began collecting details of each visitor's device and sending nothing to automated browsers, which hides it from many scanners 8. Of 169 infected Magento 2 installs missing at least one core patch, 102 also held files uploaded through PolyShell or SessionReaper, an older Magento flaw fixed in APSB25-88 8.

Four checks, then the patch

Run these from the shop's root folder. The first two look for files, the third for the script in the database, the fourth for admin accounts you did not make 68.

find pub/media/custom_options/ pub/media/customer_address/ -type f ! -name '.htaccess'
find . -name 'accesson.php' -type f

Any .php, .phtml or .phar file in pub/media/custom_options/ marks a break-in 6. accesson.php is a backdoor the March attackers planted under assets/images/ in many top folders (app/, lib/, pub/, vendor/ and others) 6.

SELECT block_id, identifier, update_time FROM cms_block
WHERE content LIKE '%fpCode%' OR content LIKE '%se_referrer%'
   OR content LIKE '%localStorage.getItem%';
SELECT user_id, username, email, created FROM admin_user ORDER BY created DESC;

Run the first query on cms_page too, and add your table prefix if the shop uses one; update_time shows the attacker's last write 8. If any check finds something, deleting the script is not the end: Sansec states the attacker keeps database access, and lists new database, admin and API integration passwords as the next step 8.

The patch: APSB26-73 ships a zip per version line, and each applies only to the newest security release of its line, so a shop first moves to 2.4.8-p5, 2.4.7-p10, 2.4.6-p15, 2.4.5-p17 or 2.4.4-p18 4. The bulletin fixes 14 flaws, not only this one, and its list of affected versions includes 2.4.9; the zip for 2.4.9 is 2-4-9-jul-2026.zip 34. On Adobe Commerce Cloud the fix also comes in the latest cloud-patches update, and Adobe notes that applying the isolated patch on top can make installation fail 4.

Until the patch is in, block the upload folder

Sansec's server rules stop an uploaded PHP file from running; they do not stop the upload, which only a firewall rule on the API call itself does 6. For nginx, placed before any \.php$ block:

location ~* ^/pub/media/custom_options/ {
    deny all;
    return 403;
}

For Apache, pub/media/custom_options/.htaccess holds:

<IfModule mod_php.c>
    php_flag engine 0
</IfModule>
Deny from all

On a hosted shop, the host or agency runs these steps; the questions to send them are the Magento version with its -p number, whether APSB26-73 is applied, and what the four checks returned.

entry.title: Lovable's agent tools have no rate limit: a Postgres cap that also stops double writes
entry.summary: Lovable's docs say its agent tools have no rate limit or call quota and no call log. A Postgres function caps calls per user, records each call, and turns a retried write into a no-op. Tested 27 October 2026.
entry.content:
Lovable can turn a published app into an MCP server: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standard that lets an AI assistant such as ChatGPT or Claude call an app's actions, which MCP calls tools 1. On 13 October 2026 Lovable added browser tools too, so an AI agent built into a browser can use the page a person has open, with that person's session 2. Lovable's own documentation, read today, answers three questions a founder should ask before switching this on 1:

QuestionLovable's answer 1
Is there a rate limit or a call quota?"Not today." Sign-in ties calls to a user but does not limit how often they call.
Can I see tool calls?No. Tool errors appear in the app's logs; successful calls do not.
Does a tool call cost anything?No separate charge. It runs in your backend, and AI or backend usage counts against your app's balance.

The same page warns that an assistant may retry a call after a timeout, so a tool that creates something can create it twice, and it suggests a request identifier 1. Three gaps, one cause: the app has no memory of who called what, when.

What the gap costs: a signed-in user's assistant can loop on your credits

Sign-in is the default for agent integrations, and a public, no-login integration needs an explicit choice 1. Sign-in does not help with volume. An assistant that misreads a task can call summarize_document again and again in one session, and every call that uses an AI model spends your app's balance. A retry after a timeout can place the same order twice. Neither shows up anywhere unless the tool fails.

The fix is one table and one function in the app's Postgres database, called at the top of each tool that costs money or writes data.

The fix: one table, one function, one call per tool

This is for apps whose backend is a Supabase project, where auth.uid() returns the ID of the signed-in caller 4. Paste it into the Supabase SQL Editor:

create table public.tool_calls (
  id bigint generated always as identity primary key,
  user_id uuid not null,
  tool text not null,
  request_id text,
  called_at timestamptz not null default now(),
  unique (user_id, tool, request_id)
);
create index tool_calls_recent on public.tool_calls (user_id, tool, called_at desc);
alter table public.tool_calls enable row level security;

create or replace function public.take_tool_call(
  p_tool text, p_request_id text, p_limit int default 20, p_window interval default '1 hour')
returns text
language plpgsql security definer set search_path = ''
as $$
declare
  uid uuid := auth.uid();
  n int;
begin
  if uid is null then return 'no-user'; end if;
  perform pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(uid::text || p_tool));
  if p_request_id is not null and exists (
    select 1 from public.tool_calls
    where user_id = uid and tool = p_tool and request_id = p_request_id) then
    return 'repeat';
  end if;
  select count(*) into n from public.tool_calls
  where user_id = uid and tool = p_tool and called_at > now() - p_window;
  if n >= p_limit then return 'limited'; end if;
  insert into public.tool_calls (user_id, tool, request_id) values (uid, p_tool, p_request_id);
  return 'ok';
end $$;

revoke execute on function public.take_tool_call from public, anon;
grant execute on function public.take_tool_call to authenticated;

Line by line, for the parts that matter:

  • Row-level security on, no policies. Row-level security (RLS) is the Postgres rule set that decides which rows each caller may read or write. With it on and no policy, the public and signed-in keys read nothing from tool_calls; only the function writes there.
  • security definer with an empty search_path. The function runs with its owner's rights, so it can write the table the caller cannot. Supabase's docs require a pinned search_path for such functions and recommend the empty one, with every table named by schema 3.
  • The two last lines. Supabase lets any role call a new function by default, including anon, the role for requests with no user session 3. The revoke and grant leave it to signed-in users only.
  • The advisory lock. Two calls from the same user to the same tool wait for each other, so two parallel calls cannot both read "19" and both pass.
  • The request ID. A second call with the same ID returns repeat and writes nothing.

In the tool's code, before the work:

const { data: verdict, error } = await supabase.rpc('take_tool_call', {
  p_tool: 'summarize_document',
  p_request_id: input.request_id ?? null,
});
if (error || verdict === 'no-user') return { error: 'Sign in first.' };
if (verdict === 'limited') return { error: 'Limit: 20 an hour. Try again later.' };
if (verdict === 'repeat') return { result: 'Already done for this request.' };

The Supabase client here has to carry the user's session, or auth.uid() is empty and every call comes back no-user. The request ID comes from the tool's own input, described to the assistant as "a unique ID for this request, the same on retries"; for a tool where the same inputs mean the same job, a hash of the inputs works.

The tool_calls table is the missing call log: one row per allowed call, with user, tool and time. A query in the SQL Editor shows who calls what:

select tool, user_id, count(*) as calls, max(called_at) as last
from public.tool_calls
where called_at > now() - interval '1 day'
group by tool, user_id order by calls desc limit 20;

Tested in Postgres 17.5: 20 of 25 calls through, retries and anonymous calls stopped

We ran the SQL above, unchanged, in PGlite, a build of Postgres that runs inside Node.js 5, on 27 October 2026. Two stand-ins replaced what Supabase provides: the anon and authenticated roles, and an auth.uid() that returns a test user ID.

TestResult
User A, 25 calls with new request IDs20 ok, 5 limited
User A, request 3 sent againrepeat
User B, first callok
No signed-in userno-user
User A, calls aged 61 minutes, new callok
Can anon execute the function?no
Can authenticated execute it?yes

The check itself is cheap. On a hosted database the cost is one round trip from the tool to Postgres, which the tool makes anyway to do its work.

Three things to set per tool

  • The limit and window. 20 an hour suits an AI summary; a read-only lookup may need none. p_limit and p_window are arguments, so each tool sets its own.
  • Which tools get the check. Lovable starts browser tools with ones that read or are easy to undo, and adds tools that delete, pay, send, publish or share only on request 1. Those requested tools, and any tool that calls an AI model, are the ones to wrap first.
  • Apps on Lovable's built-in backend. The SQL is for Supabase projects. For the built-in backend, the same three parts (a per-user count in a time window, a request ID, a row per call) can be asked of Lovable in the project chat, then checked against the table above.

entry.title: DeepSeek Flash 1017 on Workers AI: 40% faster than 0731, 23% more tokens, same bill
entry.summary: DeepSeek says its 17 October update writes shorter answers. On 10 builder tasks run 3 times each on Workers AI, 1017 finished in 40% less time than V4 Flash 0731 but wrote 23% more tokens; the lower price kept the bill level.
entry.content:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 answers in less time than V4 Flash 0731 on Cloudflare Workers AI, but it does not write less. On 10 short builder tasks, run 3 times each on 26 October 2026, 1017 took 40% less time with thinking on and wrote 23% more tokens. A token is the unit a model reads and writes, about three quarters of an English word, and the unit both models are billed in. The bill came out level, because Cloudflare charges less per token for 1017.

DeepSeek compares 1017 with a version Workers AI does not list

DeepSeek released V4.1 Flash 1017 on 17 October 2026 with open weights under the MIT licence. Its release note promises "faster task completion, and shorter outputs than the previous version" 1. The model card calls 1017 a minor update to V4.1 Flash, the 10 September release, and its benchmark table compares those two 2. V4.1 Flash is a mixture-of-experts model, one that uses a small part of itself for each token: 552 billion parameters in all, 8 billion active while reading the prompt and 16 billion while writing 3.

Cloudflare's Workers AI, a service that runs open models on Cloudflare's servers and bills per token, lists three DeepSeek V4 models: V4 Flash 0731, V4 Pro 0813 and V4.1 Flash 1017. It does not list the 10 September V4.1 Flash 56. A Workers AI user who upgrades moves from 0731 to 1017, and DeepSeek's numbers do not cover that step. We measured it.

Both models answered all 120 runs correctly

The 10 tasks are the small jobs a builder hands a model: a VAT total in baht, days between two dates, Sundays in 2027, a cron line (the schedule format servers use), an SQL query (a question to a database), a LINE order message turned into JSON (data in labelled fields), a Thai national ID check written in Python, a bug fixed in a Fibonacci function, a three-host logic puzzle and a monthly token bill. A script graded each answer: it compared numbers, ran the SQL against a test database, parsed the JSON and ran the Python against test cases.

Each task ran 3 times on each model, once with thinking off and once with it on: 120 runs. Thinking is the hidden reasoning a model writes before its answer; Workers AI counts those tokens in the output it reports and bills. With thinking on, both models used Workers AI's default effort, high 56. The runs went through the Workers AI chat completions endpoint from Chiang Rai, two at a time, between 06:40 and 06:44 Bangkok time.

30 runs per model0731, thinking off1017, thinking off0731, thinking on1017, thinking on
Correct30303030
Output tokens, total3,3624,4309,51511,664
Longest output, tokens5345449921,835
Seconds, total472711670
Seconds, median run1142
Cost, US dollars0.005530.006060.014690.01497

Seconds are whole seconds per run, as the request log records them. Cost uses the Workers AI list prices of 26 October 2026, below.

1017 writes faster, and writes more

With thinking on, 1017 wrote 2,149 more tokens than 0731 (23% more) and finished in 46 fewer seconds (40% less). With thinking off, it wrote 32% more and took 43% less time. Its longest output was 1,835 tokens, against 992 for 0731. The time saved comes from speed per token, not from fewer tokens. The model card describes speculative decoding, in which a small draft guesses several tokens ahead and the model checks them in one step 3; whether that is the cause, we did not test.

On these tasks, then, the release note's "shorter outputs" claim did not hold against 0731. It may hold against the 10 September version, which we could not run, and on the long agent tasks DeepSeek measured 1.

One number is unexplained. With thinking on, Workers AI billed 4,848 input tokens for the 30 prompts on 0731 and 3,258 on 1017, for the same prompts. With thinking off, both were billed 2,478. The cause is unknown.

The lower price absorbs the extra tokens

Per million tokens, 26 October 2026InputCached inputOutput
V4 Flash 0731US$0.44US$0.014US$1.32
V4.1 Flash 1017US$0.30US$0.006US$1.20

Both need a paid Workers AI plan 4. 1017 costs 32% less per input token and 9% less per output token. At our volumes that left the bill level: US$0.49 per 1,000 runs with thinking on for 0731 and US$0.50 for 1017; with thinking off, US$0.18 on 0731 and US$0.20 on 1017. A job that sends long prompts, such as an assistant that answers from a shop's web pages, gains more from the input price than these short prompts did.

Switching is one line

The model name is the only change. The chat_template_kwargs field turned thinking off in our runs; it is a field on the Workers AI model page 5.

curl https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$CF_ACCOUNT_ID/ai/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CF_API_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "@cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017",
       "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Days from 26 October 2026 to 14 February 2027?"}],
       "chat_template_kwargs": {"thinking": false}}'
  • A job that waits on the answer (a chat reply, a form check) gets about 40% faster on 1017 at the same cost.
  • A job billed in bulk, such as cleaning thousands of rows, costs about the same; with thinking off it costs 10% more on short prompts.
  • A cap on output tokens set for 0731 needs headroom on 1017: its longest output here was 85% longer.

Hongdam's bulk file service cleans, sorts or summarises thousands of rows with an AI model 7.

entry.title: 16,326 Supabase databases let anyone read their tables: check yours in two minutes
entry.summary: UpGuard counted 16,326 Supabase databases where anyone with the public key can read the tables. This note shows a two-minute check for your project, the SQL that closes the hole, and what Supabase changes on 30 October 2026.
entry.content:
UpGuard counted 16,326 Supabase databases where anyone who holds the app's public key can read the tables 1. The study, published 24 September 2026 and updated 14 October, started from about 300,000 domains that appeared to use Supabase and found signs of personal data in more than half of the 16,326. UpGuard links the problem to how tables are made: Supabase turns on row-level security (RLS, explained next) for tables created in its Table Editor, but not for tables created through the API, which is how coding agents work 1.

Row-level security (RLS) is the rule set inside Postgres, the database Supabase runs on, that decides which rows each caller may read or change. A Supabase app includes a public key in its browser code, called the publishable key (older name: the anon key). Supabase describes it as safe to publish because it can only access what RLS allows 2. With RLS off, that key can access every row. A second key, the secret key (older name: the service_role key), bypasses RLS entirely and belongs on a server 2.

Four scans since March 2025 all found open tables

Matt Palmer's scan of Lovable projects came first: he found the flaw on 20 March 2025, completed a scan of 1,645 projects on 21 March and published on 29 May 2025 3. NVD, the US vulnerability database, lists it as CVE-2025-48757 (insufficient RLS in Lovable through 15 April 2025): published 30 May 2025, severity 9.3 of 10 as scored by MITRE, the CVE's issuer. The record is marked disputed, because the supplier holds each customer responsible for protecting its own app's data 4.

ScanPublishedSampleOpen tables found
Palmer, Lovable projects 329 May 20251,645 projects, home pages only170 projects (about 10.3%), 303 endpoints
Modern Pentest, Y Combinator startups 526 January 202671 startups with reachable Supabase databases20 exposed personal data (28%); 43 had some exposure (61%)
Symbiotic Security 62 June 20261,072 Supabase sites from Lovable, v0, Bolt.new, Replit and Windsurf39 with tables readable by the public key; 34 more with sensitive columns exposed
UpGuard 124 September 2026about 300,000 domains showing signs of Supabase16,326 databases with readable tables

The samples differ, so the percentages cannot be compared across rows. Wiz found the same problem in Moltbook, a social network for AI agents, and reported it on 31 January 2026: the project URL and public key were in the production JavaScript, RLS was not configured, and queries returned 1.5 million API tokens and 35,000 email addresses. One PATCH request (an HTTP call that edits a record) changed an existing post, so writes were open too. The maintainer closed the tables in several steps within hours 7.

Two checks show whether anyone can read your app's data

The Connect dialog in the Supabase dashboard shows the project URL and the publishable key 2. This request asks for one table that the app uses, with the placeholders replaced:

curl -s "https://YOUR-REF.supabase.co/rest/v1/orders?select=*&limit=3" \
  -H "apikey: YOUR_PUBLISHABLE_KEY"

Rows in the reply mean every visitor to the site can read that table. [] means the key can access no rows (RLS on with no policy, or an empty table). A 42501 permission error means the table is not exposed to the key at all 8.

The SQL Editor in the same dashboard checks every table at once:

select c.relname as table_name,
       c.relrowsecurity as rls_on,
       has_table_privilege('anon', c.oid, 'select') as anon_can_read
from pg_class c
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace
where n.nspname = 'public' and c.relkind in ('r','p')
order by rls_on, table_name;

A row with rls_on false and anon_can_read true is a table the public key reads. Both checks run against your own project.

The fix: turn on RLS, take away the public role's access, and add one policy per action

alter table public.orders enable row level security;
revoke all on public.orders from anon;

create policy "owner reads own orders" on public.orders
  for select to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);

create policy "owner adds own orders" on public.orders
  for insert to authenticated
  with check ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);

auth.uid() returns the signed-in user's id; wrapping it in select lets Postgres evaluate it once per statement instead of once per row 9.

We ran these statements on 24 October 2026 on Postgres on our own computer (PGlite 0.5.11, Postgres 18.6) with test versions of the anon and authenticated roles, not on a hosted Supabase project. Before, the public role read every order. After, the public role got permission denied, user 1 read only user 1's rows, and an insert naming user 2 failed with a row-level security violation.

A policy that says true opens the table again

A policy of using (true) matches every row for every caller. Palmer reports that the scanner Lovable released in April 2025 checked that a policy exists, not what it says 3. Lovable's documentation lists rules that let everyone through among its quick scan's database checks, and says the scans find common issues, not all of them 10. On the same test Postgres, a table with a using (true) policy returned its row to the anon role. One query lists the policies that match:

select tablename, policyname, cmd
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'public' and (qual = 'true' or with_check = 'true');

On 30 October 2026 Supabase changes the default for new tables; existing tables keep their settings

A Supabase changelog entry of 28 April 2026 says new tables in the public schema are no longer reachable through the Data API (the generated REST layer that supabase-js calls) until a grant allows it. New projects get the new default from 30 May 2026, in a rollout over a few weeks; the entry sets 30 October 2026 for existing projects, six days after this note. Existing tables keep their grants and stay reachable, and RLS works as before. The entry gives the reason: agents, CLI scripts and AI platforms create tables without a human reviewing the change 8. The new default does not close tables that are already open; the check above shows which ones are.

An existing project can adopt the new default before 30 October with two statements from the same entry 8. On our test Postgres, a table made afterwards returned permission denied to anon, the older table stayed readable, and an explicit grant select made the new one readable again.

alter default privileges for role postgres in schema public
  revoke select, insert, update, delete on tables from anon, authenticated, service_role;
alter default privileges for role postgres in schema public
  revoke usage, select on sequences from anon, authenticated, service_role;

An event trigger (a Postgres rule that runs when the database structure changes) can turn on RLS for each table created afterwards, whichever tool made it. Supabase publishes its own version 11; this shorter one ran in the same test and caught both create table and create table as:

create function rls_on_new_tables() returns event_trigger
language plpgsql security definer set search_path = pg_catalog as $$
declare t record;
begin
  for t in select * from pg_event_trigger_ddl_commands()
           where command_tag in ('CREATE TABLE', 'CREATE TABLE AS', 'SELECT INTO')
             and schema_name = 'public'
  loop
    execute format('alter table %s enable row level security', t.object_identity);
  end loop;
end $$;

create event trigger rls_on_new_tables on ddl_command_end
  when tag in ('CREATE TABLE', 'CREATE TABLE AS', 'SELECT INTO')
  execute function rls_on_new_tables();

Tables created before the trigger need alter table … enable row level security run on them manually 11.

Two more problems: columns the browser can write, and secret keys in the browser

On Linkable, a paid site built with Lovable, Palmer sent a POST request with no authorization header and inserted a record with payment_status set to "paid", bypassing Stripe 3. A column the browser may write is a column a visitor may set. Column-level grants remove the write access: on our test Postgres, a signed-in user's insert or update of plan got permission denied, while display_name stayed writable.

revoke insert, update on public.profiles from authenticated;
grant insert (id, display_name), update (display_name) on public.profiles to authenticated;

The server that receives the payment provider's event then writes plan with the secret key, which bypasses RLS 2. That key in a browser bundle defeats every policy above. Supabase answers a secret key sent from a browser with a 401 error, and says a leaked key still works from other tools 2. In a framework such as Next.js, a NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix on a variable name sends its value to the browser:

NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=sb_publishable_...   # sent to the browser
SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY=sb_secret_...                          # server only: no prefix

grep -r "sb_secret_" dist build .next/static over a build folder finds a new-format secret key left in it. You replace a leaked secret key in the dashboard under Settings, API Keys 2. Supabase is deprecating the anon and service_role keys by the end of 2026 and replacing them with the publishable and secret keys 2.

entry.title: PHP2Shell: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two flaws that let attackers run code
entry.summary: Two PHP flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, let an outsider run code on a web server without logging in. PHP released fixes on 21 October 2026. Attacks began on 17 October. Updated servers also need a restart.
entry.content:
PHP, the language many websites run on, has two flaws in its core that let an outsider run commands on a web server without logging in. PHP released fixes on 21 October 2026 1, four days after Amazon recorded the first attack attempt 6. Sansec credits the exploit (attack code) that combines both flaws, called PHP2Shell, to the research firm Calif 15.

A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) number is the public ID of one flaw. A SAPI (server API) is the way PHP connects to a web server. php-fpm is a pool of PHP worker processes that nginx or Apache sends requests to; mod_php runs PHP inside Apache's own processes.

Two CVEs, both rated 9.2 out of 10, let attackers run code on the server

CVE-2026-109618: a request that exhausts memory_limit makes PHP abort while it is starting up, and the cleanup that follows treats half-built data as valid 2. CVE-2026-109619: state from one request keeps pointing at memory that request owned, and a later request on the same worker (the process that handles requests) uses the freed memory 3. Both lead to remote code execution (RCE: an outsider runs commands on the server) with the web worker's privileges 23.

PHP scores each 9.2 on CVSS v4, a 0-to-10 severity scale, with attack complexity rated high 23. NVD adds a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 for CVE-2026-109618 4. The PHP Foundation states that a score of 10.0 that circulated before the release was wrong 5.

mod_php is the most exposed setup; php-fpm depends on the application

PHP's advisory lists five affected setups: Apache mod_php, php-fpm, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. It rates mod_php highest, because an unauthenticated request reaches the first flaw before any application code runs 1, and the advisory demonstrated it with default memory and input limits 2.

For php-fpm the sources differ:

  • CVE-2026-109618: the advisory's source analysis calls FPM susceptible but shows no full exploit; FPM exits the worker when startup fails 2.
  • CVE-2026-109619: FPM is exposed through a frontend that passes PHP_VALUE settings, or through session upload progress, which was validated 3.
  • Calif demonstrated FPM behind nginx where the application decodes data after startup (session_start(), unserialize()) and lists pre-login code execution on WordPress 7.1.2, Drupal 11.4.3 and Joomla 6.1.4 16.
  • Red Hat: reliable exploitation needs precise heap manipulation, and FPM workers exit on early failure 12. Sansec: a researcher found public proofs of concept fail on default installs and mostly need a separate file-inclusion bug in the target 15.

The advisory does not cover servers without PHP or machines that run PHP only for command-line scripts; it covers PHP that serves web requests 1. RHEL 7 is not affected by CVE-2026-109618, only by CVE-2026-109619 12.

Attacks began on 17 October, four days before the fix

Amazon's honeypot network (decoy servers that record attacks) logged the first attempt on 17 October from an anonymization network. On 21 October between 02:00 and 08:00 UTC more attempts arrived with varied payloads, which suggests several attackers; Amazon cannot say whether any would have worked on a real system 6. Cloudflare saw attack traffic against customers before the release and switched on managed WAF rules (web application firewall rules, which filter requests) for Free and paid plans at 03:02 UTC on 21 October 17.

The PHP team says the CVE ids leaked about 15:00 UTC on 20 October, a demonstration video followed that evening, and the release moved from 22 October to 21 October, 14:00 UTC. It found no working public exploit at release 5. The alert from CISA (the US government's cybersecurity agency), published 21 October and revised 23 October, reports no successful exploitation observed 7. The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, version 2026.10.23, lists neither CVE (read 24 October 2026) 8.

php -v shows the command-line PHP; the web server can run a different one

A small PHP file on the web server can print which PHP build serves web requests. PHP_VERSION holds the version string and PHP_SAPI the server API name 22; fpm-fcgi is php-fpm, apache2handler is the Apache module, cgi-fcgi is FastCGI and litespeed is LiteSpeed 23. Red Hat points to a temporary phpinfo() page for web settings, because php -i reports the command-line configuration 12.

php -v                                              # command-line build only
echo '<?php echo PHP_VERSION, " ", PHP_SAPI, "\n";' | sudo tee /var/www/html/ver-check.php
curl -s https://example.com/ver-check.php           # e.g. 8.3.36 fpm-fcgi
sudo rm /var/www/html/ver-check.php

On the server itself:

ps -eo pid,lstart,user,args | grep -E 'php-fpm|apache2|httpd|lsphp|frankenphp|php-cgi' | grep -v grep
sudo apachectl -M | grep php            # mod_php loaded into Apache
grep -rn fastcgi_pass /etc/nginx/       # which php-fpm socket nginx uses

Distribution packages keep an older upstream number with a new suffix, so a printed version can read lower than the release table below while the package carries the fix; CloudLinux names alt-php85 8.5.11-5 and ea-php84 8.4.26-2.el8.cloudlinux.1 as fixed builds 14. Package versions decide.

apt list '?installed ?name(^php[0-9.]+$)'                                  # Debian, Ubuntu
zgrep CVE-2026-109618 /usr/share/doc/php8.3-common/changelog.Debian.gz    # Debian, Ubuntu
rpm -q --changelog php-common | grep CVE-2026-109618                       # RHEL family

The changelog checks come from Sansec 15. CloudLinux notes its native PHP 8.2 and 8.3 changelogs omit the CVE ids; there rpm -q php-cli reads 8.2.35 or 8.3.36 or later 14.

Four PHP versions (8.2 to 8.5) have a fixed release; 8.1 and older depend on the vendor

8.28.2.3531 Dec 2026

8.6.0RC4 carries the fix; earlier 8.6.0 builds do notnot released

Sources: 12324. The patch replaces the way PHP jumped out of the code on an out-of-memory error with a soft stop at the next safe point and a hard process exit at a higher limit 2.

Linux distributions (Ubuntu, Debian, Red Hat) use their own version numbers for the fix:

SystemPackageFixed version or erratum
Ubuntu 26.10php8.58.5.9-0ubuntu2.1
Ubuntu 26.04php8.58.5.4-0ubuntu1.5
Ubuntu 24.04php8.38.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.13
Ubuntu 22.04php8.18.1.2-1ubuntu2.28
Ubuntu 20.04, 18.04 (Ubuntu Pro)php7.4, php7.27.4.3-4ubuntu2.29+esm5, 7.2.24-0ubuntu0.18.04.17+esm14
Debian 13php8.48.4.27-1~deb13u1 (DSA-6574-1)
Debian 12php8.28.2.35-1~deb12u1 (DLA-4848-1)
RHEL 10php, php8.48.3.36-1.el10_2, 8.4.27-1.el10_2
RHEL 9php:8.2, php:8.3, php 8.0RHSA-2026:87072, 87079, 87151

Sources: Ubuntu 9, Debian 11, Red Hat 13. Red Hat's data, checked on 24 October 2026, lists the RHEL 9 php:8.4 stream as affected with no erratum 13. On cPanel hosts, ea-php82 to ea-php85 builds with the fix became stable on 21 October, and builds numbered 8.2.35-1, 8.3.36-1, 8.4.27-1 and 8.5.12-1 followed on 23 October 14.

The update is the fix; the restart is what makes it apply

PHP's advisory calls the update the only complete fix 1; a running worker keeps the code it started with. Ubuntu states that updating the packages is not enough on its own; unattended-upgrades (on by default since Ubuntu 16.04) applies security updates within about 24 hours, and applications still need a restart or the system a reboot afterward 10. Red Hat states a reload is not enough and a container is replaced, not restarted in place 12.

# Debian, Ubuntu
sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade '?name(^php[0-9.]+$)'
sudo systemctl restart php8.3-fpm       # php-fpm; unit name follows the branch
sudo systemctl restart apache2          # mod_php
# RHEL family
sudo dnf upgrade 'php*'
sudo systemctl restart php-fpm          # php-fpm
sudo systemctl restart httpd            # mod_php

The apt upgrade and the apache2 restart follow Ubuntu's notice 10; the Red Hat unit names follow Red Hat's bulletin 12. On cPanel hosts CloudLinux names /scripts/restartsrv_httpd and /scripts/restartsrv_apache_php_fpm 14.

If you cannot update yet, PHP lists partial measures, which it says do not make an install safe: session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and, on 8.5, fatal_error_backtraces=0, set in php.ini or the pool config (not ini_set() or .user.ini) with a restart; memory_limit=-1 through php_admin_value; a lower post_max_size 1.

Checking that no process still runs the old code

sudo needrestart -r l                   # Debian, Ubuntu: lists services on outdated code, changes nothing
sudo dnf needs-restarting -s            # RHEL family: services started before an updated package
for p in $(pgrep -f php-fpm); do sudo ls -l /proc/$p/exe; done
ps -o pid,lstart,args -C php-fpm8.3     # start times later than the upgrade

needrestart -r l reports services that need a restart and makes no change 19. needs-restarting -s limits its report to systemd services whose process predates an updated package 20. A /proc/PID/exe link ending in (deleted) marks a process started from a binary that has since been replaced 21; php-fpm and php-cgi are their own binaries, while mod_php lives inside Apache, so the Apache service is the one that carries it.

CVE-2026-115560 affects updated builds in one configuration

PHP's 23 October notice names a third CVE, in session upload progress, that Cloudflare states affects patched versions including 8.5.12 17. It needs session.serialize_handler set to php_binary or php_serialize, an application that switches it to php with ini_set() before session_start(), and upload progress turned on. The temporary fix is session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular release, which carries the full advisory 1; Red Hat states the setting fully addresses it 12.

Signs of a break-in: the sources list few

  • PHP's advisories list no indicators of compromise, and state that clean logs do not prove safety 3.
  • CISA names PHP worker processes launching shells or downloading tools, and points to its SIGMA detection rule 7.
  • Amazon names the string PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS in multipart POST bodies and lists six source addresses on shared anonymization networks 6.
  • The advisory's log audit looks for repeated warnings before target scripts run, fatal errors, and "Maximum execution time exceeded" 3.
  • Sansec reports a path that returns freed worker memory in a PHPSESSID cookie; that memory can hold passwords, session tokens, API keys and TLS private keys 15.

On hosted sites, the hosting company applies the fix

  • The version: WordPress lists the server setup under Tools, Site Health, Info, Server 18; the ver-check.php file above works through a host's file manager; a hosting control panel's PHP setting shows the branch it serves.
  • The fix is the host's build. CloudLinux's builds for cPanel hosts keep old numbers while carrying the fix, so a panel reading 8.4.26 can be patched 14. Cloudflare states that patching means the vendor's PHP update, not only site code or plugin updates, and that a host which manages PHP applies it 17.
  • Versions: 8.2.35 is the oldest fixed upstream release, and 8.2 security support ends 31 December 2026 124. PHP 8.1 and older receive no upstream update; vendors backport the fix or the site moves to a newer version 1. CISA lists taking a PHP system offline if it cannot be updated, or if it runs PHP 8.1 or earlier 7.
  • Cloudflare's managed WAF rules for both CVEs run by default on Free and paid plans, as an added layer beside the update 17.

entry.title: One workflow, 30,000 runs a month: Zapier US$1,149, Make US$116, Cloudflare Workers US$5
entry.summary: Zapier charges per action, Make per module, n8n per run. One order workflow at 30,000 runs a month costs US$1,149 on Zapier, US$116.47 on Make, €144 on n8n and US$5 as code on Cloudflare Workers. Prices as of 24 October 2026.
entry.content:
One order workflow costs US$5 a month on Cloudflare Workers and US$1,149 on Zapier at 30,000 runs. A workflow is a chain of automatic steps, and a run is one pass through it; Zapier, Make and n8n are tools for building workflows. The workflow is the same; each platform counts a run in a different unit, and the unit decides the price.

The example run is one trigger and four actions across three apps

In the example, a web form posts each order to a webhook, a web address that passes the order's data to the workflow. The workflow finds the customer in a Google Sheet, writes the order as a row, emails a confirmation from Gmail and posts a message in Slack. Volumes are 300, 3,000 and 30,000 runs a month, or 10, 100 and 1,000 a day. Prices are list prices taken from each vendor's pages on 24 October 2026, for the lowest plan or tier that covers the volume, not including the fees of Google, Slack or an email provider. Euro prices are converted to US dollars where compared, at the European Central Bank reference rate of 23 October 2026, EUR 1 = US$1.1193 17.

One run is 4 tasks, 5 credits, 1 execution, 1 request or 1 minute

  • Zapier counts a task for each successful action. The trigger and built-in steps (Filter, Formatter, Paths, Delay) count 0 12. The run is 4 tasks.
  • Make counts a credit for each module action, and reading an incoming webhook is one of them. Router and error-handler modules count 0 34. The run is 5 credits. Make's pricing page dates the switch to credits as its billing unit to 27 August; its help pages say operations.
  • n8n counts a run of the whole workflow at any number of steps: "An execution is a single run of your entire workflow." 5 The run is 1 execution.
  • Cloudflare Workers is code that Cloudflare runs for each incoming request, so you rent no server. It bills requests, and calls the code makes outward are free. The paid Standard plan also bills CPU time, the processor time the code uses; waiting on the network does not count 67. The run is 1 request.
  • GitHub Actions bills minutes on its runners, with each job rounded up to a whole minute 89. A job that ends in seconds is 1 minute.

Per-step counting grows with the workflow. One more action moves Zapier from 4 to 5 tasks (a quarter more) and Make from 5 to 6 credits (a fifth more). n8n stays at 1 execution, and a Worker adds milliseconds of CPU time, which fall within the 30 million included at these volumes 6.

At 30,000 runs, Zapier costs about 10 times Make and 230 times Cloudflare Workers

Zapier, Professional 14 tasksUS$58.50 (1,500-task tier)US$283.50 (20,000-task tier)US$1,149 (200,000-task tier)
Make, Core 35 creditsUS$10.59 (10,000-credit tier)US$18.82 (20,000-credit tier)US$116.47 (150,000-credit tier)
n8n Cloud, Starter then Pro 51 execution€24 (Starter, 2,500 executions)€60 (Pro, 10,000)€144 (Pro, 50,000)
n8n self-hosted, Community Edition 510111 execution€5.99 to €26.99 server, plus update hours€5.99 to €26.99 server, plus update hours€5.99 to €26.99 server, plus update hours

Annual billing lowers Zapier to US$39, US$189 and US$769, Make to US$9, US$16 and US$99, and n8n Cloud to €20, €50 and €120 135. The Free plans do not cover the example run: Zapier's Free plan allows two-step Zaps and 100 tasks, Make's Free plan covers 200 runs in its 1,000 credits, and n8n Cloud starts with a trial limited to 1,000 executions 135. GitHub Actions starts a job from an event, which an outside form can send with a repository_dispatch call 18; standard runners in a public repository cost nothing 8.

Workers Free limits each request to 10 ms of CPU time. Cloudflare reports about 2.2 ms for the average Worker and 10 to 20 ms for heavier ones, such as authentication or large payloads 7. The example run's CPU time is not measured here, so the table shows both plans.

n8n self-hosted: a €5.99 to €26.99 server plus update hours

Self-hosting means running n8n's free Community Edition on a server you rent and update yourself 5. Hetzner lists a 2 vCPU (virtual processor core), 4 GB server at €5.99 a month excluding VAT at its NBG1 and HEL1 locations (CX23), and a 2 vCPU, 4 GB AMD server at €19.99 at those locations and €26.99 at SIN1 in Singapore (CPX22) 1011. The order line on both pages read "currently unavailable" on 24 October 2026. n8n's Hetzner guide asks for at least 4 GB and 2 vCPU once its Assistant feature is added 12. The load is small: n8n's benchmark puts one instance at up to 220 executions a second, and 30,000 runs a month average 0.012 a second 13.

The server price is the smaller part. An update is three commands, docker compose pull, docker compose down and docker compose up -d 14. Read from GitHub on 24 October 2026, n8n published 26 releases, on 17 different days, in the 30 days to that date, and 29 security advisories on two days: 14 on 30 September and 15 on 14 October, 15 medium and 14 high severity 1516. At one hour per update window (time to update and test the workflow), those two days come to 2 hours a month. The hour is an assumption, not a measurement; no source times it.

With more steps, Make costs more than n8n Cloud

  • A ten-credit run (a trigger and nine actions) at 30,000 runs needs 300,000 Make credits, US$214.31 a month on Core, while n8n Cloud Pro stays at €144 (US$161.18) 35.
  • Up to 200 runs a month, Make's Free plan covers the example workflow at US$0. At 300 runs the lowest paid tiers are Make US$10.59, n8n Cloud €24 (US$26.86) and Zapier US$58.50.
  • A daily job such as a price check is 30 runs a month. Zapier's lowest Professional tier (750 tasks, US$29.99), Make's lowest Core tier (US$10.59) and n8n Starter (€24) each cover it 135.
  • Code on Cloudflare Workers or GitHub Actions has no per-step unit; its cost is the time to build and maintain it. Hongdam's price is ฿8,000 a workflow: one trigger, up to three apps, an alert when it stops and 30 days of fixes, in n8n, Make, Zapier or code, with the tool's own fees charged at the price we pay 19.
